[EFFECT] The year feature has a clear, step-change effect on predicted demand: hours in 2011 (yr = 0) pull the model's prediction *down* — typically by a contribution of around −0.15 to −0.50 in log space — while hours in 2012 (yr = 1) push it *up*, with contributions clustered around +0.10 to +0.30. In other words, all else being equal, the model predicts noticeably more bike rentals in 2012 than in 2011. Because this is a binary feature, there is no gradual transition — it is simply a before/after shift between the two years.

[IMPORTANCE] Year is the **2nd most important** feature in the model (out of 9), with an importance score of 0.200 — very close to temperature (ranked 3rd at 0.197) but substantially weaker than the hour of the day (ranked 1st at 0.833). It is a significant driver of demand predictions, capturing what appears to be overall year-over-year growth in ridership.

[RECOMMENDATION] Since the model has learned that ridership was systematically higher in 2012 than in 2011, you should account for long-term growth trends in your planning: if ridership continues to grow year over year, fleet sizes, docking capacity, and staffing levels may need to be scaled up accordingly — rather than assuming past-year figures reflect current demand.
